title: Simple sorts
objective: Sort like cards in your hand (insertion sort), and see why it slows down on big inputs.

sources.title: Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest and Stein, Introduction to Algorithms, 4th ed. (MIT Press, 2022): insertion sort

simplifies: Bubble and selection sort are the other classic simple sorts; they are also O(n²). Insertion sort is shown because it is fast on nearly-sorted input, where few items need to move.

quiz.prompt: Insertion sort on a list that is already sorted does…

options.text: No slides at all, just one comparison per item
options.explanation: Right. Each new item is already in place, so it is O(n) on sorted input.
That happens on a reversed list, where every pair is out of order.
It runs; it just has nothing to move.

quiz.prompt: In the worst case, insertion sort on n items does about how many slides?

options.explanation: Right. A reversed list has n(n − 1)/2 out-of-order pairs, and each needs one slide.
That is the best case, not the worst.
Comparison sorts can't do that well: there are n! possible orders to tell apart.
